analysis.one_liner: Narrows Endangered Species Act habitat protections around reservoirs, canals, and water delivery facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill to limit Endangered Species Act protections around western reservoirs and canals died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have weakened several parts of the Endangered Species Act as they apply to dams, reservoirs, canals, and other water delivery structures. It would bar the government from designating man-made, fluctuating reservoir habitat as protected critical habitat, let agencies count conservation offset projects when judging harm to habitat, lower the legal bar for approving wildlife mitigation plans, and exempt water facility operators from liability when endangered aquatic species are harmed by non-native species someone else introduced.
analysis.who_benefits: Operators of water storage reservoirs, diversion structures, and canals — including irrigation districts, municipal water agencies, and dam operators — would face lower compliance costs under the Endangered Species Act and gain immunity from liability in a specific set of circumstances involving non-native species.

how_it_helps.text: Bars designation of critical habitat within the high-water mark of reservoirs, canals, and other artificial water facilities when the habitat is created and destroyed by fluctuating water levels, removing a source of regulatory obligation for facility operators [S2][S3].

Requires the Secretary to count offsetting habitat conservation measures, including alternative habitat, when determining whether a federal action would harm critical habitat — easing approval of water projects [S2][S3].

Deems the mitigation requirements for incidental take permits satisfied whenever the Secretary finds the proposed measures are merely 'rationally related' to the level of take, a looser standard than current practice [S2][S3].

Exempts water facility operators from liability for harm to listed aquatic species when that harm stems from predation or competition by non-native species introduced by someone else into the river basin [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Endangered fish and other aquatic species in western river basins, and the broader public interest in species protection, would bear the cost through reduced habitat safeguards and weaker mitigation requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Endangered aquatic species and their habitats

drawbacks.text: The bill removes critical habitat protection for man-made reservoir and canal habitat that listed species actually use, weakening a core protection of the Endangered Species Act for western aquatic species [S2][S3].

Lowering the mitigation standard to 'rationally related' gives agencies wide discretion to approve projects with thin conservation offsets, and the non-native species exemption could shield operators from responsibility for harm that is hard to attribute precisely to who introduced a species.

A good-faith objection supporters would raise: the bill responds to a real grievance, since designating artificially fluctuating reservoir habitat as critical habitat can impose compliance costs on water agencies without producing much conservation benefit, and operators can be blamed for damage caused by invasive species they did not introduce.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to water facility operators in the form of reduced regulatory exposure, while the costs fall on habitat protection for listed species and on the credibility of the mitigation process. The bill does address a genuine friction between western water operations and the Endangered Species Act, but it settles that friction almost entirely in the operators' favor rather than through balanced conservation requirements.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Flake of Arizona introduced the bill on April 26, 2005, joined by four additional Arizona Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources [S1][S3][S4][S5].
Three days after introduction the House requested an executive comment from the Interior Department, but the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S5].
The action history shows no further movement after the Interior comment request; the bill remained in committee until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Endangered species protections came out ahead: the existing critical habitat, mitigation, and liability rules for water facilities stayed exactly as they were, and water facility operators did not obtain the exemptions they sought.

for.name: Rep. Jeff Flake
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to limit critical habitat designation and ESA liability for water facilities.

for.name: 5 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (all Arizona Republicans: Hayworth, Renzi, Shadegg, Franks, Flake)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original sponsors from the Arizona delegation.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Richard Pombo
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Arizona Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill never advanced far enough to produce a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Water storage and delivery operators (irrigation districts, municipal water agencies, canal operators)
industries.note: The bill would have freed these operators from critical habitat obligations inside their facilities, eased mitigation requirements, and exempted them from take liability for harm caused by non-native species. Their regulatory savings come directly at the cost of habitat protection for listed species that the public owns an interest in.

industries.industry: Dam and diversion structure operators, including hydropower
industries.note: Excluding fluctuating reservoir zones from critical habitat and loosening the mitigation standard would reduce the regulatory burden of operating and relicensing dams, reducing constraints on project operations that affect fish habitat.

industries.industry: Environmental conservation and species protection interests
industries.note: The bill would have narrowed critical habitat designations, softened mitigation review, and created a liability carve-out — each a rollback of tools conservation groups rely on to protect listed aquatic species.
